en: The General Meaning of the Thirty-nine Chapters of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha:
Now, as for the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, it is the ocean of the nature of all Buddhas, the single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
It reveals the subtle and profound sublime expositions and unfolds the inexhaustible essential purport. In terms of its vastness, there is nothing it does not encompass.

As for its precision and subtlety, there is nothing it does not encompass. Although it may be entered through a single path or a single gate, its thousand distinctions and myriad transformations are inexhaustible.
Those who gaze upon it cannot fathom its channels; those who approach it cannot perceive its boundaries.
It is as if one were to take the vast ocean to make ink and gather Mount Sumeru to form a brush, yet still be unable to exhaust the meaning of a single phrase.
How much more so for those with shallow and superficial views who do not even recognize its lowly aspects, yet desire to explore its profound mysteries?
If there were no systematic threads to follow, by what means could one penetrate its essential meaning?

In the first assembly at the site of enlightenment, when our Buddha, the World-Honored One, first attained perfect awakening, he manifested the wondrous essence of Vairocana, making his body coextensive with the entire Dharma-realm.
He revealed the adornments of both the environment and its inhabitants, equal in measure to the great void.
These are designated as forty kinds of adornments; each category possesses an infinite and boundless number of features, equal to the atoms within ten buddha-fields.

The Bodhisattvas surrounded him on all sides. Furthermore, forty classes of divine beings and their retinues—each leading countless, immeasurable, boundless, and peerless ocean-like multitudes—gathered like clouds to celebrate the Dharma King’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment.
In total, there are four hundred and twenty verses praising the Buddha’s inconceivable ocean of merit and vows;

each verse individually reveals a dharma-gate for realizing the Way. Altogether, there are four hundred names of Bodhisattvas and celestial deities who serve as lords of the world and provide the adornments of the dependent retribution.
Therefore, it is called "Wondrous Adornment. This chapter, established at the beginning, is the first.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs": This signifies that from between the teeth of the World-Honored One’s face, he emitted rays of light as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field;
each ray, in turn, had rays of light as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field as its retinue.
Within these rays of light, there appeared infinite lands, infinite Buddhas, and infinite Bodhisattvas. Thus it was awakened.
He realized that throughout all worlds, all sentient beings had resolved their minds upon Bodhi and were born into the family of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, he emitted a brilliant light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which universally illuminated the boundless lands of the ten directions, manifesting infinite adornments.

Boundless bodhisattvas appeared simultaneously within the radiance. Furthermore, before the World-Honored One, a great lotus flower emerged, endowed with inexhaustible adornments and perfected by various jewels;
upon it sat the assembly of bodhisattvas, each praising the Buddha’s merits with verses.
The Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Samādhi signifies that the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, seated upon a lion throne within the Lotus Treasury before the Tathāgata,
enters the Sarvabuddha-Vairocana-Tathāgatagarbha-kāya-samādhi, whereby he is able to manifest himself before all the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, in worlds as numerous as the atoms within the infinite Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
He teaches the Dharma with his own body and turns the sublime wheel of Dharma.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of Worlds": this represents the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s universal observation of the oceans of all worlds, the oceans of all assemblies, the oceans of all Buddhas, the oceans of all dharma-realms, and the oceans of the karma of all sentient beings, as well as their faculties.

The Ocean of Desire. The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, by means of ten kinds of knowledge, knows all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings, teaching and transforming them to bring them to fulfillment and benefit them, causing them to enter the realm of the Buddha.

Furthermore, he manifests the oceans of worlds, each with its own adornments, each with its own basis of abiding, each with its own shape, each with its own mode of entry, each with its own radiance, and each with its own essential characteristics.
They abide for various eons; each is distinct, with individual forms, and each possesses ten times the number of names and characteristics as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
The "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World" represents this very center of the fragrant water ocean, named Boundless Sublime Flower Light.
From it emerges a great lotus flower named Calyx-Fragrance Banner Flower Treasury World-Ocean, which dwells therein.
It is surrounded on all sides by ten times unspeakably many fragrant water oceans, as numerous as the atoms within ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. There are ten times unspeakably...
The world-seeds abide therein. Within them are lotus ponds, jewel-śīla banners, pavilions, bell-nets, city-walls, groves, trees, and sandalwood enclosures;
each is individually adorned with unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of ornaments, pervading everywhere.
Each ocean of fragrant water contains as many oceans of fragrant water as there are atoms in the four continents.
The rivers wind to the right in a circular course. Each river is adorned with ten unspeakable numbers of atoms of dust;
their substance, magnitude, and shape each have ten unspeakable varieties. All of these are distributed and abide within this Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean.
Within this central fragrant water ocean, there are ten unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.
Within these worlds, as numerous as atoms, they are arrayed. Within a single ocean of fragrant water, twenty tiers of world-systems are situated.
The first tier of world-systems at the very bottom consists of worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, surrounding it on all sides.
The second tier of world-systems consists of worlds as numerous as the atoms in two buddha-fields, surrounding it on all sides.

They surround it, increasing in layers upon layers. Just as with the twentieth world-system seed, there are worlds numbering as many as the atoms within twenty buddha-fields that surround it; this constitutes the first set of twenty layers.
Furthermore, ten sets of twenty layers surround this first set of twenty layers, and one hundred sets of twenty layers surround these.
There are eleven layers of twentyfold [worlds]. To speak extensively, there are ten unspeakable numbers of such twentyfold layers, joined and arranged exactly as described in the sūtra.
Regarding the "Vairocana Chapter," it represents the Buddhas of antiquity in order to illustrate the present Buddha; there is a sea of fragrant water.

It is named Pure Light. There is a world named Supreme Sound. Within that world is a great forest named Mani Flower Branch Wheel, adorned with various ornaments in infinite variety and immeasurable in its vastness.
There is a great forest city where a king of men resides, surrounded on all sides by a hundred trillion nayutas of cities. Within this city dwell...

There are people who have not failed to achieve accomplishment; through the supernatural power of karmic retribution, they travel back and forth through the air, their conduct identical to that of the devas.

Within this Great Forest of Jewel Flower Branch Wheels, there is a site of enlightenment named Jewel Flower Universal Illumination, adorned with a distribution of various great jewels extending throughout the ten directions. Before this site of enlightenment lies a great ocean named Fragrant Maṇi Gold.
Suddenly, there emerged a great lotus flower named "Flame-Wheel of Petal-Kernels. This flower was vast, measuring one million *yojanas* in breadth;
its stalk, leaves, filaments, and calyx were all composed of wondrous jewels. It was surrounded by ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of lotus flowers.
Within the first eon of this world-system of Supreme Sound, there were [Buddhas] as numerous as the atoms in ten Mount Sumerus...
He appeared in the world. The first of these Buddhas was named Sumeru-Vijaya-Cloud of All Merit Mountains.

He suddenly manifested within a great lotus flower at his place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). His body was all-pervasive, equal to the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and he manifested his birth in every buddha-field, appearing at all places of enlightenment and proceeding to them all. This was in the world-system known as Supreme Sound.
There were sixty-eight thousand billion peaks of Mount Sumeru. Upon each one, he manifested his body and sat.
From the space between his eyebrows, he emitted a great radiance, with light rays as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields serving as its retinue, filling all the lands of the ten directions.
All sentient beings who encountered this light immediately attained self-awakening through that flaming radiance.
In that great city there was a king named Priyadarśana-Sudhīmat (Joyous Vision and Good Wisdom), who ruled over a hundred trillion nayutas of cities.

Among the king’s sons, queens, and court ladies, there were five hundred princes headed by Mahātejas (Great Splendor), ten thousand queens headed by Sudarśanā (Beautiful Vision), and sixty thousand ministers headed by Prajñābala (Power of Wisdom). It was thus.
Together with a multitude of seventy-seven hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* beings, they went as one to see the Buddha. Immediately, they realized ten kinds of Dharma-gates.
Various articles of offering filled the entirety of space. Upon reaching the place where the Buddha was, they performed their respects and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, for the sake of taming all sentient beings, that Tathāgata, within the assembly at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), [proceeded to teach].

He preached the *Sūtra on the Universal Collection of the Sovereign Dharmas of All Buddhas of the Three Times*, with the *Sūtra on the Ocean of Worlds* as its retinue, causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit according to their inclinations. At that time, the Buddha Victorious Cloud remained in the world for fifty billion years.
After the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, there appeared a second Buddha, a third Buddha, and a fourth Buddha, each succeeding one after another.
In this world, the king, the crown prince, the various ministers, and the people approached him in succession, obtained benefit, realized the Way, and became great Bodhisattvas.
This section of the sutra text indicates that by citing ancient Buddhas, it serves as a testimony for the present Buddha;

the Dharma of Vairocana Tathāgata’s appearance in the world has been handed down from antiquity to the present, remaining unchanged across all ages. Thus concludes the section from the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of World Rulers" up to...
This, together with the six chapters of the sūtra text, constitutes from beginning to end a representation of the adornments within the Bodhimaṇḍa;

it represents the general outline of the ritual for attaining enlightenment and preaching the Dharma by Buddhas of the past and present, held within a great assembly comprising bodhisattvas, divine beings, the eight classes of supernatural beings, devas, nāga kings, human kings, and the lords of the world. Furthermore, this one-quarter [of the entire work]...

This constitutes the completion of the first cycle of the "Factor of Faith. Furthermore, one cycle of the five cycles constitutes the completion of the cycle of the "Object of Faith," which consists of cause and effect.
Upon reading the scripture to this point, one may understand the sequential order.

The "Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas" signifies that in the second assembly, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne of the precious lotus-flower treasury in the Hall of Universal Radiance.
Manifesting great supernatural powers, he brought forth a resonance that pervaded the Dharma-realm.

At that assembly, within the Bodhimanda, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields raised thirty-two kinds of inquiries regarding the causes and conditions of the Dharma, desiring to inspire them toward the awakening of bodhicitta.
Regarding the "lifting of the mind": it causes one to know the vast practices and vows of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.

Furthermore, their names and titles manifest their numerical extent as being equal to and pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Within this Sahā world, across the four continents, there are various distinct names for each [Buddha].
Moreover, within a single direction of the worlds of the ten quarters, there are ten thousand names, each distinct and different.
Furthermore, within this Sahā world-system, there are ten billion sets of four continents;
therein, the Tathāgata possesses ten trillion various names and titles, causing all sentient beings to know and perceive him individually.
Moreover, outside of this Sahā world-system—in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—within each of these ten directions, there are ten million [worlds].
There are billions of various names and titles, causing all sentient beings to know and see them individually, as explained at length in the sutra.
Throughout all worlds within the entirety of empty space and the pervasive dharma-realm— worlds that are incalculable, immeasurable, inconceivable, unfathomable,
and unspeakably unspeakable in number, beyond all limits— there are [names] that cause all sentient beings to know and see them individually, as [the sutra describes].
The *Sūtra* itself contains the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," which indicates that within this Sahā world, four kinds of noble truths are taught.
The first kind is designated by ten names, while the other three kinds are each designated by forty names; these are distinct from one another in this world.
Within this world-system, there are four hundred billion and ten thousand names explained in detail, which serve to tame all sentient beings according to their needs.
Likewise, in each of the worlds throughout the ten directions, there are four hundred billion and ten thousand names.
Thus, in every single world throughout the entirety of space and the pervasive Dharma-realm in the ten directions, the Four Noble Truths are likewise taught.
Each possesses four hundred billion ten-thousand names, which, according to the minds of sentient beings, cause them all to be tamed, as described in the aforementioned scriptural passages.
This collectively explains the inexhaustible names throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions; all have the Four Noble Truths as their essence.
From these Four Noble Truths, various Dharma gates are differentiated, within which the five aggregates and the twelve links of dependent origination are all fully contained.
Within this are also included the eighty-four thousand liberations from afflictions (*kleśa*), as explained at length in the sutras.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Radiance of Enlightenment": it signifies that from beneath the wheels on the soles of the World-Honored One’s feet, he emitted ten billion rays of light, illuminating ten billion Jambudvīpas, ten billion Pūrvavidehas, and ten billion Aparagodānīyas within this trichiliocosm.
Yajñeya, there are ten billion Uttarakurus, ten billion great oceans, ten billion Cakravāḍa mountains,
ten billion bodhisattvas taking birth, ten billion bodhisattvas renouncing the household life, ten billion Tathāgatas attaining perfect enlightenment,
ten billion Tathāgatas turning the wheel of Dharma, ten billion Tathāgatas entering parinirvāṇa, ten billion Sumeru mountains, and ten billion Four Great Kings.
The three-and-thirty heavens numbering in the hundreds of millions, up to the Akaniṣṭha heavens numbering in the hundreds of billions—
all that exists therein appeared clearly. Just as here one sees the Buddha, the World-Honored One, seated upon a lion throne within a Lotus Treasury,
surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, so too did the hundred billion Tathāgatas appear within the hundred billion Jambudvīpas.

They sat in this manner. By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions, there arrived at the place where the Buddha was a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields. Their names were Mañjuśrī, Daśaśiras Bodhisattva, and others.
The lands from which they came were the Golden World (*Suvarṇabhāsa*) and others. The Buddhas whom they served were...

The Buddhas of Immovable Wisdom and the others. At that time, Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously uttered verses in the presence of each Buddha, praising the ten kinds of dharmas of the Buddhas with ten stanzas to cause those with faith to awaken their enlightened nature and believe that they themselves are the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom. Thereupon, the light passed beyond this world.
It shines universally upon ten Buddha-lands in the eastern direction; it is likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Within each of those worlds, there are ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens;
everything therein is clearly manifested. The light passes beyond ten worlds and shines universally upon one hundred worlds in the eastern direction.
The same applies to the four intermediate directions, above, and below. The light passed beyond a hundred worlds and universally illuminated a thousand worlds in the eastern direction;
the same applies to the four intermediate directions, above, and below. The light passed beyond a thousand worlds and universally illuminated ten thousand worlds in the eastern direction.
The light passed beyond ten thousand worlds and universally illuminated a hundred thousand worlds in the eastern direction. The light passed beyond a hundred thousand [worlds].
The world. He illuminates a million worlds to the east; the four intermediate directions, above, and below are likewise so.
Even his radiance extends beyond ten billion worlds, illuminating a hundred billion worlds and a thousand billion worlds to the east.
A nayuta, a hundred nayutas, a thousand nayutas, and a hundred thousand nayutas of worlds—
in each of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, it is likewise so. Thus,
they are innumerable, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, and unspeakable, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
As it is with all worlds within the realm of empty space, so it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Within each of those individual worlds, there are ten billion Jambudvīpas, and so on, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens.

All appeared clearly. Within each and every Jambudvīpa, the Tathāgata was seen sitting upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.
From each of the ten directions, a great bodhisattva arrived before the Buddha, each accompanied by a multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

As for the great Bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī and others, the lands from which they have come such as the Golden World (*Suvarṇabhāsa*), and the Buddhas whom they originally served such as Akṣobhyajñāna Buddha and others—in all these places, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and his peers simultaneously uttered verses at the feet of their respective Buddhas to praise them.
This was to cause those who had not yet developed faith to give rise to it, and to cause those who already possessed faith to advance in their practice. These are the ten [points].
Within the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), one establishes one hundred and forty kinds of great vows and accomplishes the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), Wisdom-body (*prajñākāya*), and Knowledge-body (*jñānakāya*) advance simultaneously, thereby perfecting the ten gates of faith as fully elucidated in the sutra.
The "Chapter on the Inquiry into Clarity" (Prajñāparipṛcchā-parivarta) represents the inquiry by Mañjuśrī into Bodhisattva Awakening Chief (Bodhimukha), Ten Chief (Daśamukha), and others.
[It asks: "O Son of the Buddha, the nature of the mind is one; why is it seen to have various distinctions? That is to say: going to good or evil destinies;
the completeness or deficiency of the sense faculties; similarities and differences in rebirth; being handsome or ugly; the disparity between suffering and pleasure; and [the diversity of] karma."
The mind does not know the mental objects; sensation does not know its retribution; retribution does not know sensation; the mind does not know sensation; sensation does not know the mind;
the cause does not know the condition; the condition does not know the cause; wisdom does not know the object; the object does not know wisdom.
Bodhisattva Chief of Enlightenment answered in verse:
You now ask about this meaning in order to awaken the multitude of living beings;
I shall answer according to its nature—O Benevolent One, you should listen attentively. All phenomena lack functional activity and possess no intrinsic nature;
therefore, they are all entirely unable to know one another, just like the waters in a river.
Filling and flowing, they rush and hasten together, each unaware of the others; so too are all phenomena.
Furthermore, like a great mass of fire, fierce flames erupt simultaneously, each unaware of the others;
so too are all phenomena.
The teachings given in response consist of ten verses in total, answering the questions as they are fully contained within the sutra itself.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī questioned the ten "Chief" Bodhisattvas—Vasumukha, Ratnamukha, Guṇamukha, Netramukha, Vīryamukha, Dharmamukha, Bhadramukha, and Vīryottaramukha—and each of these ten Chief Bodhisattvas responded to Mañjuśrī with ten verses of their own. These are the teachings given in response.
The verses are not recorded here. There are one hundred questions in total, and there are likewise one hundred answers, as fully contained within the sutra itself.
Regarding the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," it represents Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressing Jñānacūḍa Bodhisattva, saying: "O Son of the Buddha."

You have now asked about this meaning out of a desire to bring great benefit and great peace to the world, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake of the welfare and happiness of devas and humans.
If all bodhisattvas skillfully employ their minds, they will obtain all supreme and wondrous merits.
Regarding all Buddha-dharmas, their minds are without obstruction; they abide in the path of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, dwelling among sentient beings and never forsaking them.
They are able to thoroughly penetrate the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are, severing all evil and becoming fully endowed with all virtues.

One should become like Samantabhadra, foremost in physical appearance, fully endowed with all practices and vows, and possessing sovereign mastery over all phenomena, acting as a second teacher for sentient beings. How should one apply the mind so as to attain all supreme and wondrous merits?
Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva is at home, they should wish that sentient beings realize the empty nature of the household and escape its [bondage].
When passing through narrow passages, one should wish that all beings serve their parents with filial piety, skillfully serving the Buddha and nurturing all sentient beings.
When gathered with wife and children, one should wish that all beings regard enemies and kin with equanimity, forever remaining free from greedy attachment.

When approaching teachers, whether great or small, one should wish that all beings skillfully serve their elders and superiors, practicing and cultivating wholesome dharmas. Furthermore, upon seeing the Buddha, one should wish that all beings...
One attains the unimpeded eye and beholds all Buddhas. These, along with the remaining one hundred and forty great vows, serve to perfect the mind of practice within the stage of the Ten Faiths.

Although this is a conditioned mind, it is nonetheless able to perfect the ocean of wisdom, principle, and great compassion within the subsequent five stages. All subsequent entry into the ocean of myriad practices proceeds from this.
This can be accomplished through the superior power of the conditions of one hundred and forty great vows.

As for the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (Bhadramukha-parivarta): having already set forth the great merit of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s pure conduct free from turbidity and confusion, [the text] now seeks to reveal the merit of the bodhicitta; therefore, it asks the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha in verse:
Now, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, I shall speak of the pure conduct practiced by the Buddha in the past;
you, O Benevolent One, should likewise expound upon the supreme merits of such practice within this assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha replied in verse:
Excellent! O virtuous one, you should listen attentively. Those merits are immeasurable;
I shall now describe a small portion according to my ability, Like a single drop of water from the great ocean.
If there is a bodhisattva who first resolves their mind, Vowing to seek the realization of Buddha-enlightenment.
His merit is boundless, Incalculable and beyond compare;
How much more so throughout immeasurable and infinite eons, As he fully cultivates the stages, the perfections, and all virtues!
All the Tathāgatas of the ten directions Together praise it, yet can never exhaust it.
Such are these boundless great merits; I now describe but a small portion therein.
It is like the space traversed by a bird’s feet, Or like a single mote of dust upon the great earth.
These four preceding verses clarify that the merit of generating the bodhicitta is vast and immeasurable; they provide a brief description according to one's capacity in order to illustrate it.
Because the bodhicitta cannot be measured by limits, its merits shall likewise be so. Hereafter, there are in total three hundred and seventy-two verses.

Their general purport is to praise in summary the faith of those who have generated the bodhicitta, causing them to practice with firm resolve and remain free from all negligence. Furthermore, this is the second assembly, the Samantaprabhā...
In the Hall of Radiance, he preached the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths, consisting of six chapters of sutra, completing one full cycle from beginning to end.
Furthermore, there were three assemblies. The assembly at the summit of Mount Sumeru in the palace of Śakra was called the Assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

The chapter titled "Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru" symbolizes the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, whereby in each of the four continents of every world throughout the ten directions—
Throughout Jambudvīpa in the world, all saw the Tathāgata sitting beneath a tree.
Each had a bodhisattva who, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, expounded the Dharma; none failed to feel as though they were constantly in the presence of the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One, without leaving his seat beneath the Bodhi tree at every location, ascended Mount Sumeru and proceeded toward the palace of Śakra. There, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, was present.

Before the Palace of Sublime Victory, he saw the Buddha approaching from afar. Immediately, by means of his supernatural power, he adorned this palace and prepared a lion throne within the Treasury of Universal Radiance.
That throne was composed entirely of exquisite jewels, adorned with ten thousand tiers and ten thousand golden nets of various kinds.
Ten thousand princes and ten thousand Brahma kings surrounded it in front and behind, along with ten thousand rays of light.
It was bright and radiant. At that time, Śakra, having respectfully prepared a seat for the Tathāgata, bowed with palms joined and paid homage toward the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you will, out of compassion, dwell in this palace. Immediately, the World-Honored One entered the Palace of Sublime Victory (*Abhyudgata-vimāna*).
In all worlds throughout the ten directions, it was likewise so. Furthermore, he praised the Buddha’s merits with ten verses.
The practices and vows are as fully set forth in the sutra itself.
Regarding the "Chapter on Verses of Praise on Mount Sumeru," it manifests the Buddha’s spiritual power;

thus, from each of the ten directions, there comes a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, [arriving] from [a distance of] one hundred buddha-fields.
From world-systems outside as numerous as the atoms of dust, they gathered in assembly. Their names were Bodhisattva Dharmamati, Bodhisattva Sarvajñānamati, and others.
The worlds from which they came were the Indra-jāla world and others. The Buddhas whom they served were the Buddha Viśiṣṭacandra and others.
Once these Bodhisattvas had arrived at the place of the Buddha, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet and, according to their [respective...]
From each direction, they each manifested a lion throne of the Vairocana-treasury and sat upon them with legs crossed.

In all worlds throughout the ten directions, it was likewise. At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of wondrously colored light from his two big toes, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions, including the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, atop Mount Sumeru.
The Buddha and the great assembly were all fully manifest. At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"In this manner, the ten wisdom-bodhisattvas each praised the Buddha’s meritorious virtues, practices, and vows with ten verses each, as detailed in the sūtra itself.
Altogether there are one hundred verses, extolling the signless as the ultimate reality. This concludes the section.
One realizes the dharma of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), causing all mental and physical calculations to have no basis for reliance. Free from biased attachments, one dwells where the Buddhas dwell.
The verses have not been recorded; they are fully contained within the sutra itself.
The "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" represents the Bodhisattva Dharmamati. Receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, he entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Immeasurable Expedient Means.
By the power of this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions...
There were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a thousand buddha-fields, all bearing the same name: Dharmamati.
They appeared before him and addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying: "O son of noble family, you have been able to enter this samādhi.
All the Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, together empower you with their spiritual power. Furthermore, it is by the power of Vairocana..."

By the power of the vows and the majestic spiritual authority of Vairocana Tathāgata in the past, and by the power of the roots of goodness you have cultivated, you are enabled to preach the Dharma for the sake of increasing the Buddha-wisdom.
When the Bodhisattva Dharmamati arose from his meditative concentration, he addressed the bodhisattvas:
"Sons of the Buddha, there are ten abodes of bodhisattvas, which the Buddhas of the past, present, and future have already taught and will continue to teach."

Now it shall be explained. What are the ten? They are: the Dwelling of Initial Resolve, the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground, the Dwelling of Practice, the Dwelling of Noble Birth, the Dwelling of Fulfilling Skillful Means, the Dwelling of Rectified Mind, the Dwelling of Non-retrogression, the Dwelling of Youthful Truth, the Dwelling of the Dharma Prince, and the Dwelling of Empowerment.
These are called the Ten Dwellings of a Bodhisattva. Within the Dharma of the Ten Dwellings taught by the Buddhas of the two periods, these are the meritorious practices.
The rules are as contained in the sūtra itself.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Holy Life" (*Brahmacarya-varga*): it represents the Devaputra Samyaksmṛti addressing the Bodhisattva Śukladharmamati, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, how do the assemblies of bodhisattvas in all worlds, having donned the dyed robes and left the household life in reliance upon the Tathāgata’s teaching, attain the holy life?"
Purity. From the stage of a bodhisattva until the attainment of the path of unsurpassed enlightenment, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati said:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva practices the pure conduct (brahmacarya), they should take ten things as their objects of focus and observe them with mental attention.
These are: the body and bodily action; speech and verbal action; the mind and mental action; and the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and precepts. One should contemplate them in this way: the body is..."
Is it the holy life (*brahmacarya*)? Or even, is it the precepts that constitute the holy life?
If these were the holy life, one should know that the holy life would then be non-virtuous, contrary to the Dharma, turbid, foul-smelling, and impure.

[This applies to] the three types of action, the six sense faculties, the five aggregates, the twelve links of dependent origination, the eighteen elements, the six supernormal powers, the three types of higher knowledge, and the four immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Measuring the mind through the six pāramitās, one does not give rise to dualistic interpretations regarding all phenomena. Thus, all Buddha-dharmas swiftly manifest before one.
At the very moment of the initial resolve for enlightenment, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Knowing that all dharmas are the self-nature of the mind, one accomplishes the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*), as this is not realized through another. Within this, ten dharmas are distinguished and explained.
The various meanings and terminology are as fully contained in the sutra itself.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Merits of First Generating the Bodhicitta," it represents Śakra Devendra addressing the Bodhisattva Śukladharmamati, saying: "O Son of the Buddha!"
"When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, what is the measure of the merit thereby obtained?

The Bodhisattva Dharmamati replied, "This meaning is extremely profound; it is difficult to explain, difficult to know, difficult to discern, difficult to believe and understand, difficult to realize, difficult to practice, difficult to penetrate, difficult to measure, and difficult to enter. Nevertheless, I shall now speak for you by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic power."

O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were someone who, for the duration of one kalpa, provided all manner of articles of pleasure to all sentient beings in as many incalculable worlds in the eastern direction as there are, and subsequently taught them to purely observe the five precepts; [and suppose they did likewise] in the southern, western, and northern directions.
The same applies to the four intermediate directions, above, and below. If this were continued for an entire kalpa, would such merit not be great?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied: "Compared to the merit of a bodhisattva’s initial resolve, this person's merit does not equal even a hundredth part or a thousandth part."
It is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy. The illustrations explained therein are so numerous and extensive that they are difficult to exhaust;
their number is recorded in the sutras and may be known by reading them. They extensively clarify that the merit of generating the bodhicitta is immeasurable.
As fully contained within the sutra itself,
the "Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma" represents the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha addressing the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying: "O Son of the Buddha,
when a bodhisattva first resolves to seek omniscience, they accomplish immeasurable merit and are endowed with great adornment, ascending to the first..."
The vehicle of all-encompassing wisdom. Entering the correct stage of the bodhisattvas, they abandon all worldly dharmas and attain supramundane dharmas.
They are definitively sustained by the Buddhas of the three periods of time until they reach the state of unsurpassed enlightenment. At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati...

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vīramati: "Excellent, son of the Buddha! You now desire to bring great benefit, great peace, and great welfare to many, out of compassion for the world, by inquiring about such a Dharma.

Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva abides in ten kinds of non-negligence, they attain ten kinds of pure dharmas. These are extensively and clearly explained in the sutras, as the sutra itself states."

Complete. In general, by firmly maintaining the pure precepts, diligently cultivating secret practices, extensively delivering sentient beings, and perfecting the power of wisdom, one realizes that the Buddhas of the three periods of time share a single essence due to the purity of the mind.

The above three assemblies—from the summit of Mount Sumeru to the celestial palace of Śakra—symbolize the "Chapter on the Summit of Mount Sumeru," symbolize the "Chapter of Verses of Praise," symbolize the "Chapter on the Ten Stages," and symbolize the Brahma [Heaven].

The Chapter on Practice (*Caryā-parivarta*), the Chapter on Manifesting the Merits of the Initial Resolve (*Prathamacittotpāda-guṇa-vyūha-parivarta*), and the Chapter on Manifesting the Dharma (*Dharmavyūha-parivarta*):

these six chapters of the sūtra constitute the first cycle from beginning to end of the third assembly, serving as the section of "Explanation" (*vyākhyāna*). Within the cycle of the differentiated causes and effects, one can discern the sequence by reading the sūtra up to this point.
The Fourth Assembly: The Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. This signifies the majestic spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata;
thus, without departing from beneath the Bodhi tree or the summit of Mount Sumeru, he proceeded to the Palace of Jewel Adornments in that Yāma Heaven.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven saw the Buddha approaching from afar and, by means of his own spiritual power, within his palace—
He manifested a lion throne within a treasury of precious lotuses, adorned with one million tiers and interlaced with one million golden nets.
Each of these various adornments numbered one million, extending even to the radiance that shone forth.
One million kings of the Yāma Heaven paid homage by bowing their heads in reverence, along with one million Brahmā kings and one million bodhisattvas.
Praising the Buddha’s virtues. At that time, the Heavenly King spoke verses in praise of the Buddha, using ten verses in each case to extol his merits.

Just as the Yāma Heavenly King in this world, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, proclaimed and praised him, so did all the Yāma Heavenly Kings in every world throughout the ten directions do likewise.
Regarding the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven": it manifests the Buddha’s spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).

From worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields, one great bodhisattva from each of the ten directions—assembled together with a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within those buddha-fields—came to this assembly. Their names were: the Bodhisattva Guṇakūṭa (Forest of Merit), and so forth.

The Bodhisattvas and others from their respective lands, such as the world-system of Priyadarśana and so forth, had each purified their brahma-conduct in the presence of Buddhas, such as the Buddha Nityanetra and others.
Once these Bodhisattvas had arrived at the place of the [present] Buddha, they prostrated themselves at his feet.
In each direction from which they came, they manifested lion thrones made of mani-jewel treasuries and sat upon them in the full lotus posture.
Just as the Bodhisattvas, including the King of the Yāma Heaven, had gathered in this world, so it was in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakūṭa spoke in verse: "The Buddha emits a great radiance, Universally illuminating the ten directions."
They all beheld the Honored One among Gods and Humans, who has attained unimpeded penetration and so forth.

Thus, these ten forest-dwelling bodhisattvas each praised the Buddha’s meritorious conduct and vows with ten verses, benefiting all sentient beings and attaining the path to Bodhi; together they formed one hundred verses, as detailed in the sutra itself.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Ten Practices": it represents the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha. Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation.

Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared before him ten thousand Buddhas—as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields—all named Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, who addressed him:
The Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha said, "O Son of the Buddha, you are indeed able to enter this samādhi.

This is because the Buddhas of the ten directions are collectively bestowing their empowerment upon you, as well as through the power of the Tathāgata’s past vows and the power of the roots of goodness of the assembly of bodhisattvas."

He caused you to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma. At that time, all the Buddhas bestowed upon him ten kinds of wisdom and each extended his right hand to stroke the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha.
Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha then arose from his concentration and addressed the Bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of the Buddha, the practices of a Bodhisattva are inconceivable; they are equal to the realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space."
The ten kinds of practices are those proclaimed by all Buddhas of the three periods of time. What are these ten? First, the practice of joy; second, the practice of benefiting others;
third, the practice of non-contrariety; fourth, the practice of being unbending; fifth, the practice of freedom from delusion and confusion;
sixth, the practice of excellent manifestation; seventh, the practice of non-attachment; eighth, the practice that is difficult to attain; ninth, the practice...

The practice of wholesome dharmas. Tenth is the practice of reality. Regarding these ten practices, each has its own functional rules and analogies for the merit of cultivation within a single practice, which benefit sentient beings.
When this Dharma was being taught, the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways; such was the manifestation when the Ten Practices were taught in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven in this world.
Such were the supernatural transformations; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it was exactly thus.

Furthermore, each of the ten forest-dwelling bodhisattvas recounted, with ten verses each, the meritorious practices and vows within the Ten Practices, as detailed in the sutra itself, totaling one hundred verses.
Regarding the "Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries": this represents the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma-avana (Flower Forest of Merit). He addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of the Buddha, there are ten treasuries of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which have been taught by the Buddhas of the past, will be taught by those of the future, and are being taught now.
What are these ten? They are: the treasury of faith, the treasury of ethical discipline, the treasury of moral dread, the treasury of shame, the treasury of generosity, and the treasury of wisdom."
The treasury of memory, the treasury of mindfulness, the treasury of retention, and the treasury of eloquence—these are the ten.
By means of these ten kinds of treasuries, through the power of the Bodhisattva’s practice, application, and vows, all Bodhisattvas bring supreme enlightenment to ultimate fulfillment;
they also cause all worldly activities to reach the ultimate, inexhaustible great treasury. This concludes the Chapter on the Palace of the Yāma Heaven and the Chapter on Verses of Praise.
The Chapter on the Ten Practices; the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries. From beginning to end, there are four assemblies in one cycle.
The fifth is the Assembly in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. As for the "Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," it symbolizes the Buddha’s spiritual power;
thus, without departing from all locations—namely, beneath the Bodhi tree, the summit of Mount Sumeru, and the Yāma heaven—he proceeds to Tuṣita.
In the celestial palace, within a hall adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven saw the Buddha approaching from afar.
Upon that palace, he spread a lion throne of maṇi-treasury, composed of various celestial jewels,
manifested through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, and born of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of roots of goodness.
Within that palace, there were various adornments, each consisting of one hundred trillion kinds of offerings;

in total, there were one hundred eighty-four million billion such offerings. Furthermore, there were one hundred and eight million billion bodhisattvas, as well as the celestial kings, the eight classes of supernatural beings, and others, each numbering one hundred million billion in their respective assemblies.
They paid respectful homage and surrounded him on all sides. At that time, within the palace, the World-Honored One ascended the lion throne of the maṇi-treasury and sat cross-legged.

Then, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields, arriving together at the place where the Buddha was.
Their names were Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva and others. The lands from which they had come were the World of Exquisite Jewels and others.

The Buddhas whom they served were Akṣayadhvaja Buddha and others. Having arrived at the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet, and according to the directions from which they had come, each manifested a precious seat and sat cross-legged.
From each of their bodies, they emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas [of light rays].

The light shone universally throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions, manifesting great supernormal transformations that were pure and majestic, filling all of space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Just as the assembly of bodhisattvas had gathered in this Tuṣita Heaven palace of our world, so it was in every Tuṣita Heaven palace in all worlds throughout the ten directions. At that time...

"World-Honored One, from his two kneecaps, he emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of light rays that universally illumined the ten directions, throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
All those bodhisattvas in all worlds saw these signs of the Buddha’s spiritual transformations;
these bodhisattvas likewise saw the signs of the spiritual transformations of all those Tathāgatas. Thus did the bodhisattvas..."
All these [bodhisattvas] have, in the past, planted roots of goodness together with the Tathāgata, cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva, and reached the ultimate shore of great wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvāṇa; by the power of his original great vows, he manifests the Dharma of sovereign mastery.
These ten verses and others praise the Buddha’s merits. Thus, up to the Bodhisattva Daśaketu, each praised him with ten verses.
The Buddha. As fully contained within the sutra itself, there are one hundred verses.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" (*Daśapariṇāmanā-parivarta*): it represents the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, who, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, enters the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom (*jñānāloka-samādhi*).
Having entered this samādhi, he [perceives] in each of the ten directions worlds as numerous as the atoms of a hundred thousand buddha-fields.
Outside the realm, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within a hundred thousand Buddha-fields, all bearing the same name, Vajradhvaja.
They all proclaimed in praise: "Excellent, Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to enter this samādhi. This is the teaching of the Buddhas of the ten directions."

We shall collectively bestow our power upon you and expound the Dharma, so that all bodhisattvas may attain pure fearlessness, so that they may protect and uphold the lineage of the Tathāgatas, and so that they may expound the ten kinds of dedication of bodhisattvas, which have been expounded by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
What are these ten? First is the dedication to rescue and protect all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being."
1. Dedication toward [the goal]; 2. indestructible dedication; 3. dedication equal to all Buddhas; 4. dedication reaching all places; 5.
dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit; 6. dedication entering into the equality of all roots of goodness;
7. dedication in accordance with all sentient beings; 8. dedication according to the characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā).
Ninth is the dedication of liberation without bondage or attachment. Tenth is the dedication of entering the inexhaustible realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

These ten kinds of dedication have been taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time—those who have taught them in the past, those who will teach them in the future, and those who teach them now.
Within each of these dedications, there are great vows consisting of numerous and countless sections. Furthermore, there are two hundred and forty-six verses of praise that reiterate them.

Having thus set forth the great vows and merits within these ten kinds of dedication, at that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the assembly of bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions all spoke these words: "Excellent, Vajradhvaja!
You are able to expound these ten kinds of great dedications; we too shall speak them in this way throughout the worlds of the ten directions, with the same phrasing and terminology."
The meaning is entirely as such. We have gathered here to bear witness for you.
Then, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse.
Thus concludes the fifth assembly, beginning and ending with the exposition of the Dharma-gate of the Ten Transferences within this Tuṣita Heaven Palace.
The Sixth Assembly. Spoken in the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Regarding the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Ten Stages":

This indicates that the World-Honored One was in the Maṇi-ratna-garbha Hall of the Palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, together with a multitude of bodhisattvas who had all gathered there from other directions.
All merits have been fully practiced and brought to perfection; even in unspeakable eons, they could not be fully described.
With Vajragarbha Bodhisattva as the leader, they, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.
Having entered this samādhi, immediately throughout the ten directions, beyond ten billion buddha-fields...
Beyond worlds as numerous as atoms, there appeared before him ten billion buddha-fields, each containing as many buddhas as atoms, all named Vajragarbha.
They spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, Vajragarbha! You are indeed able to enter the samādhi of the light of great wisdom.
This is the collective empowerment bestowed upon you by the buddhas of the ten directions, and it is also [the empowerment] of Vairocana..."

By the power of the original vows of Vairocana Tathāgata, at that time the Buddhas of the ten directions each bestowed upon him ten kinds of wisdom and extended their right hands to stroke the crown of Vajragarbha’s head. Having thus stroked his head, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha arose from samādhi.
He addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha! The vows of all bodhisattvas are as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as space;
they extend through the limits of the future, pervading all buddha-fields to rescue and protect sentient beings.
They are protected and remembered by all Buddhas, and they enter the ground of wisdom of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present. O Sons of the Buddha! [The Bodhisattva]...

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s stages of wisdom consist of ten types. These have been taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time—those of the past, those of the future, and those of the present—and I likewise teach them now.
What are these ten? First is the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi); second is the Stage of Purity (Vimalā-bhūmi); third is the Stage of Radiance (Prabhākari-bhūmi);

fourth is the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi); fifth is the Stage Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā-bhūmi); sixth is the Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi); seventh is the... [text truncated]
The Ground of Far-Reaching Travel; eighth, the Ground of Immovability; ninth, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence; tenth, the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.
These ten grounds constitute the supreme path toward Bodhi for the bodhisattva, and they are also gateways to the light of the pure Dharma.
The merit, practice, vows, and power of these ten grounds are so vast and immeasurable that they cannot be illustrated by analogy. In the first ground, the bodhisattva mostly...
As a great king, on the second stage one mostly becomes a king of Jambudvīpa; on the third stage, one mostly becomes a wheel-turning sage-king (cakravartin);

on the fourth stage, one mostly becomes a king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; on the fifth stage, one mostly becomes a king of the Yāma Heaven; on the sixth stage, one mostly becomes a king of the Tuṣita Heaven;
on the seventh stage, one mostly becomes a king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and on the eighth stage, one mostly becomes a lord of a small thousandfold world system.
On the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), one mostly acts as the lord of a medium chiliocosm; on the tenth stage, one mostly acts as the lord of a great trichiliocosm.

The functional power and great vows of these ten stages are vast and incomparable. Furthermore, there are a total of three hundred and eighty-six verses that reiterate the merits and great vows within these ten stages, as fully contained in the sutra itself.
The seventh assembly was spoken in the Hall of Universal Radiance within the Bodhimaṇḍa. Regarding the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis":

it signifies that the World-Honored One, having first attained perfect enlightenment in the Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha, entered the Samādhi of the Limit of the Kṣaṇa in the Hall of Universal Radiance;
by means of the sovereign supernatural powers of all-knowledge, he manifested the Tathāgata’s body as pure and unobstructed, and remained therein.

Śamatha is supremely tranquil and possesses great majestic power. He was accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, all of whom had attained the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka) and had acquired the bodhisattva samādhi called "Universal Vision.
They dwelt in the bodhisattva liberation of non-abiding. Their names were Bodhisattva Vajramati and others; in former times, they had all [been with him].
When the Tathāgata Vairocana was practicing together with the Bodhisattvas in various roots of goodness, the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra dwells in the inconceivable, vast, and great samādhi of a bodhisattva;
whether emerging from or entering it, he possesses sovereign mastery over all samādhis and supernatural powers without ceasing. The Buddha told Samantacakṣus: "Now, this..."

Within this assembly, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva shall explain it for you. At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, immediately expounded ten great samādhis within the great assembly, causing all bodhisattvas of the three periods of time to fully attain great mastery.
What are these ten? First is the Great Samādhi of Universal Radiance; second is...
1. The Great Samādhi of Wondrous Light; 2. The Great Samādhi of Successively Traveling to All Buddha-lands;
3. The Great Samādhi of Pure Conduct with a Profound Mind; 4. The Great Samādhi of the Treasury of Adornments of the Past; 5.
The Great Samādhi of the Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom; 6. The Great Samādhi of Thoroughly Knowing the Buddha-adornments of All Worlds.
Samādhi. Eighth is the great samādhi of the differentiated bodies of sentient beings. Ninth is the great samādhi of mastery over the dharma-realm.
Tenth is the great samādhi of the unimpeded wheel. These ten great samādhis can be skillfully entered by the great bodhisattvas;
they have been taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. If bodhisattvas delight in practicing them, [they shall attain these states].
Then one attains accomplishment. Such a person is called a Buddha; they are called a Tathāgata; they are also called a Teacher, a Great Teacher, and the All-Knowing One.
Within these ten great samādhis, they universally encompass all sentient beings and cause them all to become pure.
By means of the wisdom of skillful means, they manifest the attainment of the Buddha-way within these ten great samādhis.
The power of its efficacy is fully contained within the sutra itself.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers": it records the Buddha’s command to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to inform all bodhisattvas that there are ten kinds of supernatural powers.
What are the ten? First, the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds; second, the supernormal power of unimpeded divine sight;
third, the supernormal power of the knowledge of past lives throughout kalpas; fourth, the supernormal power of the knowledge of all kalpas extending to the limits of the future;
fifth, the supernormal power of unimpeded and pure divine hearing; sixth, abiding in the absence of intrinsic nature.

1. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding the nature of non-action that travels to all Buddha-fields; 2. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding the manifestation of immeasurable bodies; 3. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding the mastery of all sounds and voices;

4. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding the non-dual nature of all phenomena; 5. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding the non-arising of all phenomena; 6. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding the nature of non-action that reaches all Buddha-fields; 7. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding the skillful discernment of all speech and terminology;

8. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding the infinite forms of the physical body; 9. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding all dharmas; 10. The supernormal knowledge of wisdom regarding the unimpeded understanding of all three periods of time. These are the ten kinds of supernormal powers.
By means of the power of vast majesty and sovereign mastery, as fully detailed in the sutra itself,
the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" (Daśakṣānti-parivarta) represents the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s address to all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas concerning the ten kinds of patience.
If one attains these patiences, one will reach the stage of the unimpeded patience of all Bodhisattvas and all Buddhas.

The Dharma is unimpeded and inexhaustible. What are these ten? They are: the patience of sound, the patience of conformity, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, the patience of being like an illusion, the patience of being like a flame, the patience of being like a dream, the patience of being like an echo, the patience of being like a shadow, and the patience of being like space.
These ten kinds of patience have been taught by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time; I now teach them in the same way, even as far as the tenth, which is like space.
The Bodhisattva Śūnyatākṣānti accomplishes this patience and attains a body that does not come, because it does not go, and so forth.
Furthermore, thirty-four verses restate the power of the practices, deeds, and vows within these ten patiences, as is fully contained in the sutra itself.

The "Chapter on Incalculable Numbers" (*asaṃkhyeya*) signifies that the Buddha expounded the sequence of numbers through *asaṃkhyeya* units, reaching the ultimate limit of the "unspeakably unspeakable" number, thereby enabling all worlds to enter into the meaning of the quantities known by the Buddha.
One hundred lakṣas constitute one koṭi; the number of lakṣas is here called "hundred million" (*yì*). The number of koṭis is here... [text fragment ends]
A *yun* (雲) constitutes one *zhào* (兆). Ten *koṭi*s constitute one *ayuta*. Ten *ayuta*s constitute one *nayuta*, which is here called one hundred *zhào*.

In this manner, the numbers increase tenfold at each step until reaching one hundred and twenty kinds of great numbers, culminating in the "unspeakable-unspeakable" (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*) and again the "unspeakable-unspeakable."
It constitutes one unspeakable turning; the enumeration of its names and numbers is fully contained within the sutra itself. This chapter was spoken by the Buddha himself.
As for the "Chapter on the Lifespan": it represents the Heart-King Bodhisattva addressing the various bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, one kalpa of the buddha-field of Śākyamuni Tathāgata in this Sahā world is [equal to] one day and night in the buddha-field of Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss."
One day and night in the world Sukhāvatī is one kalpa in the world Kāṣāyadhvaja;
one kalpa in the world Kāṣāyadhvaja is one day and night in the world Avivartyasvaracakranirghoṣa;
one kalpa in the world Avivartyasvaracakranirghoṣa is one day and night in the world Vimalā. One [kalpa] in the world Vimalā... is one day and night in the world... Vimalā.
One kalpa of the world-system *Kaluṣa* constitutes one day and night in the world-system *Supradīpa*.

One kalpa of the world-system *Supradīpa* constitutes one day and night in the world-system *Duranjaya*. One kalpa of the world-system *Duranjaya* constitutes one day and night in the world-system *Vibhūṣitabuddhi*.
One kalpa of the world-system *Vibhūṣitabuddhi* [constitutes one day and night] in the world-system *Ādarśaprabhā*.
One eon in the world-system *Prabhāsa* constitutes one day and night in the world-system *Ādarśaprabhā*.
Following this sequence, up to the final world-system among a million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, one eon therein constitutes one day and night in the world-system *Vimalapadma*.
This world-system is filled with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and all his fellow great bodhisattvas.

Among them, having heard this teaching, their minds were opened and enlightened; they came to know that the Buddha’s lifespan is beyond what can be known through calculation and is not within the reach of the power of the mind, as is fully detailed in the sutra itself.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas": it represents the Heart-King Bodhisattva Mahāsattva addressing the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:

"O Sons of the Buddha, in the eastern direction there is a place called Mount Ṛṣigiri, where a bodhisattva named Vajraśūra dwells constantly together with various bodhisattvas. In the southern direction there is a place called Mount Śikhin..."
There is a place named Dharmamati where he dwells together with various bodhisattvas.
To the west, there is a place named Vajrajvālācala where a bodhisattva named Vīryavīrakrama dwells together with various bodhisattvas.
To the north, there is a place named Gandhamādana where a bodhisattva named Gandhahastin dwells together with various bodhisattvas.
In the northeast there is a place called Mount Qingliang (Clear and Cool), where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī dwells together with various other bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, there is a dwelling place known as the Śāmbala Cave.
Since ancient times, the assembly of bodhisattvas has dwelt therein. Altogether, there are twenty locations where the great bodhisattvas practice.

From the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas" to the "Chapter on the Abodes of the Bodhisattvas," these twenty-six chapters of the sutra constitute the Section of Explanation (*vyākhyāna-bhāga*), forming the cycle of the differentiated causes and effects. Having read the sutra up to this point:
Only then does one understand the sequence.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharma of the Buddhas": it signifies that within this great assembly, there were various bodhisattvas who formed this thought:
"In what way are the buddha-fields inconceivable? In what way are the original vows of the Buddhas inconceivable? Various...
How inconceivable is the lineage of the Buddhas! How inconceivable is the appearance of the Buddhas!
How inconceivable is the body of the Buddhas! How inconceivable is the voice of the Buddhas! How inconceivable is the wisdom of the Buddhas!
How inconceivable is the sovereignty of the Buddhas! How inconceivable is the unimpededness of the Buddhas!

Discourse: How is the liberation of all Buddhas inconceivable? At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, empowered them through his spiritual power and illuminated them with the radiance of wisdom.

He caused the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus Treasury to abide in the fearlessness of the Buddhas, enter the Buddha-dharmadhātu, protect the majestic virtue of the Buddhas, attain mastery in supernormal powers, and obtain the [fearlessness] of the Buddhas.
Obstructing. He observes extensively and knows all Buddha-lineages, abiding in succession in the ineffable skillful means of the Buddhas' teachings.
O Son of the Buddha! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have immeasurable abodes; they possess ten kinds of dharmas that universally pervade the boundless Dharma-realm;
they have ten kinds of mindfulness, which give rise to wisdom; they have ten kinds of non-missing of the proper time; and they have ten kinds of incomparables.
In this inconceivable realm, there are ten kinds of wisdom that give rise to it; ten kinds of universal entry into the Dharma-realm;
ten kinds of vast dharmas difficult to believe and accept; ten kinds of great merit, pure and free from faults;
ten kinds of ultimate purity; ten kinds of Buddha-activities; ten kinds of inexhaustible self-sea dharmas; and ten kinds of...
It is eternally abiding. There are ten kinds of expositions of the immeasurable Dharma-gates of all Buddhas;
ten kinds of performing Buddha-works for the sake of sentient beings; ten kinds of most excellent dharmas; ten kinds of unobstructed dwellings;
ten kinds of most excellent and unsurpassed adornments; ten kinds of sovereign dharmas; and ten kinds of immeasurable, inconceivable perfections.
In the Buddha-dharma, there are ten kinds of vast buddha-activities; ten kinds of sovereign dharmas of non-dual conduct;
ten kinds of abidings that abide in all dharmas; ten kinds of knowledge of all dharmas exhaustively and without remainder;
ten kinds of great Nārāyaṇa-bannered, heroic, and vigorous dharmas; ten kinds of powers; ten kinds of swift dharmas; and ten [kinds of...]
The dwelling of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) consists of ten kinds of unimpeded liberation (*pratisaṃvid-vimokṣa*).

Based on this single chapter of the sūtra, there are ten questions at the beginning and twenty-eight answers at the end. Within each answer, ten modes of answering are contained, totaling two hundred and eighty inexhaustible phrases of response.
This is the functional power within the inconceivable dharmas of the Buddha, as described in the sūtra.
The "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata" is intended to represent the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra addressing the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, I shall now expound for you the ocean of marks possessed by the Tathāgata. Upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, there are thirty..."

There are two kinds of marks of a Great Being adorned with jewels. Among them is a mark of a Great Being named "Illuminating All Ten Directions, Universally Radiating a Net of Immeasurable Great Light," which is adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels.
Its jeweled topknot extends everywhere, being soft, supple, and dense; from each part, it emits jewel-light that fills all boundless worlds. Entirely...
The manifestation of the Buddha-body with its perfect physical marks is the first. Next is a mark of greatness called Cloud of the Radiance of the Buddha-Eye.
Next is a mark of greatness called Cloud Pervading the Dharma Realm. Next is a mark of greatness called Cloud Manifesting Universal Illumination.
Next is a mark of greatness called Cloud Emitting Precious Radiance. Next is a mark of greatness.
The name of the first manifestation of the Tathāgata’s great sovereign cloud is "Cloud of the Universal Lamp of the Tathāgata.
Next is a mark of greatness named "Cloud of the Vast Radiance Universally Illuminating All Buddhas. Next is a mark of greatness named "Cloud of Perfectly Complete Radiance.
Next is a mark of greatness named "Radiance of the Treasury of Practices Universally Illuminating All Bodhisattvas."
Yun: In this manner, throughout his entire body, there are ninety-seven kinds of marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

Each one possesses its own name, function, and vast majestic power. If explained in detail, the Tathāgata Vairocana possesses as many such marks of a Great Man as there are atoms in ten Flower Treasury World-Oceans, each upon his body.
The various exquisite marks of the jewels are divided to serve as adornments, as fully detailed in the sūtra itself.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Merit of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance," it signifies that the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, saying:
O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses a secondary mark (anuvyañjana) named King of Perfection.
From within this mark issues forth a great radiance called Blazing Intensity, which has seven million asaṃkhyeya rays of light as its retinue.
Furthermore, in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, he emits a great radiance named King of Light-Banners, which illuminates worlds as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields.
World-systems. Within those worlds, the sentient beings in the hells who encounter this light find their manifold sufferings stilled and attain ten kinds of purity;
their eyes, ears, noses, tongues, bodies, and minds likewise each attain ten kinds of purity.
They all give rise to joy, and when their lives there end, they are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s entire body possesses eighty-four thousand marks of physical excellence.
There are one thousand marks. Each mark possesses eighty-four thousand secondary signs (anuvyañjana). Within each secondary sign are eighty-four thousand rays of light.

Within each ray of light, one beholds the boundless Buddhas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, the great Śrāvakas, and the noble Sangha of the Perfect Enlightenment. Those who encounter these rays of light shall all attain the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment].
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the meritorious practices and vows within this section on the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) are fully contained within the sutra itself.

As for the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" (*Samantabhadracaryā-prakaraṇa*), it represents the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra addressing the bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha, as previously [stated]..."
What has been expounded here is merely a brief explanation of a small portion of the Tathāgata’s realm, proclaimed in accordance with the faculties and capacities of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, I do not see a single dharma that constitutes a greater fault than when Bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of anger toward other Bodhisattvas;
for this immediately results in one million gateways of obstacles. What are these one million gateways of obstacles? They are as follows: namely, failing to see...
Obstacles to awakening; obstacles to not hearing the true Dharma; obstacles to being born in impure worlds; obstacles to being born in the various evil destinies;

obstacles to being born in places of hardship; obstacles of many illnesses; obstacles of being frequently slandered; obstacles of being born dull-witted; obstacles of losing right mindfulness; obstacles of lacking wisdom;
obstacles of the six sense faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—not being acute; and obstacles of perverse knowledge.

The obstacle of consciousness; the obstacle of evil companions; the obstacle of delighting in practicing the Hīnayāna; and even the obstacle of distancing oneself from the lineage of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva gives rise to a single thought of anger toward other bodhisattvas, they will incur as many as one million such doors of obstacles.
O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva should diligently cultivate ten kinds of dharmas. What are they?
There are ten [qualities]. Namely: not abandoning any sentient being; conceiving the thought of all bodhisattvas as being Tathāgatas, and so forth.
By dwelling securely in these dharmas, one attains ten kinds of purity, namely: the purity of penetrating the profound dharma, and so forth.
Having dwelled in these ten dharmas, one becomes fully endowed with ten kinds of vast wisdom, such as the wisdom that knows the mental activities of all sentient beings.

Having dwelled in these ten wisdoms, one attains entry into ten kinds of universal entries—namely, the entry of all worlds into a single pore-path, the entry of a single pore-path into all worlds, and so forth. Having observed in this manner, one then abides.
There are ten kinds of sublime minds, namely: the sublime mind that abides in all worlds, the sublime mind regarding speech and non-speech, and so forth.
Having abided in these ten sublime minds, one then attains ten kinds of skillful wisdom regarding the Buddha-dharma, namely:
the skillful wisdom that thoroughly understands the profound Buddha-dharma, and so forth. O Son of the Buddha, having heard this Dharma, Bodhisattvas should all resolve [to attain it].
Receive and uphold this with a reverent mind. Why is this? Those who uphold this Dharma will, with little effort, swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They shall all become fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, becoming equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
While this Dharma was being spoken, in each of the ten directions there were ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta*s...
From as many worlds as there are atoms in other Buddha-fields, the earth shook in six ways, and rains of all kinds of offerings—
such as flowers, incense, robes, canopies, banners, and flags from all the heavens of the past— filled the void and pervaded the entire Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, one hundred and twenty-one verses are used to restate the preceding teachings as they appear in the sutra itself.
This Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra serves as the cause for equality.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata": it signifies that from the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows of the World-Honored One, a great radiance was emitted, named "The Appearance of the Tathāgata.
It was accompanied by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya rays of light.
These lights universally illumined the ten directions, reaching to the ends of empty space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm and all worlds. To the right...
It circled ten times, manifesting the Tathāgata’s immeasurable sovereignty and awakening countless multitudes of bodhisattvas.

It shook all worlds throughout the ten directions, extinguished the sufferings of all evil realms, eclipsed all the palaces of Māras, and revealed all Buddhas and Tathāgatas seated upon the Bodhi throne, attaining equal and perfect enlightenment. It performed...
When this was done, he circumambulated the assembly to the right and entered the crown of the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagarbha-samudgata-vimala-guṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalaguṇa joined his palms with single-minded devotion and addressed the Buddha in verse, praising the Buddha’s merits with ten stanzas.
Then, from his own mouth, the Tathāgata emitted a great radiance called “Unobstructed Fearlessness,” consisting of hundreds of thousands of billions of asaṃkhyeyas.
With light as its retinue, it universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions, the void, and the dharma-realm.
It circles to the right ten times, manifesting the various sovereign powers of the Tathāgata to awaken immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas.
Having performed these deeds until the Tathāgata sits upon the Bodhi seat and attains equal and perfect enlightenment, it enters the mouth of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

Once that light had entered, the body and seat of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, as well as those of all the other bodhisattvas, became a hundred times greater than they were before—except for the Tathāgata’s lion throne. At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagotra-vyūha-guṇa asked Samantabhadra:
"O Son of the Buddha, the great spiritual transformations manifested by the Buddha cause all these bodhisattvas to give rise to joy."

They were filled with joy. It was inconceivable; no one in the world could know what auspicious sign this was. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva said, "O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata has manifested a vast and great miraculous transformation.
He then spoke the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s Appearance, which gives rise to immeasurable light of inquiry into the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prakṛtivyūha-guṇarāja asked Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, "How does one know all..."

The manifestations of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha— his speech and sounds, his samādhis, his attainment of enlightenment, his turning of the wheel of Dharma,
